title: Explain the prevention and treatment of animal diseases

lessons.title: Causes of disease and how it spreads
lessons.html:
What causes animal disease?

A disease is any condition that stops an animal's body from working normally. On South African farms most production losses come from a small number of causes. As a supervisor you must know these causes so you can stop problems early.

Main causes

  • Bacteria - for example the bacteria that cause anthrax, blackquarter (sponsiekte), mastitis and foot rot.
  • Viruses - for example foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, bluetongue and African swine fever.
  • Parasites - internal parasites such as wireworm (Haemonchus) and tapeworm, and external parasites such as ticks, lice, mites and blowflies.
  • Protozoa carried by ticks - such as redwater and gallsickness (which is caused by a rickettsia-like organism) in cattle.
  • Nutritional and toxic causes - mineral shortages, poisonous plants such as tulp and gifblaar, and feed mistakes like bloat or acidosis.

How disease spreads

Disease moves from sick to healthy animals in several ways:

  • Direct contact, for example at a water trough or in a crowded kraal.
  • Contaminated feed, water, soil or bedding.
  • Vectors such as ticks, flies and midges.
  • People, vehicles and equipment - a bakkie that drove through an infected farm can carry mud and dung onto yours.
  • Bought-in animals that look healthy but carry disease.

Stress makes it worse

Animals under stress get sick more easily. Common stresses are drought, poor veld, cold rain after shearing, long transport, overcrowding and rough handling. Good management reduces stress and so reduces disease.

Some diseases are controlled or notifiable diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Foot-and-mouth disease, anthrax, African swine fever and others must be reported to the state veterinarian. If you suspect one of these, keep the animals where they are, stop all movement and report at once.

lessons.title: Preventing disease on the farm
lessons.html:
Prevention is cheaper than treatment

A dead or sick animal costs the farm money in lost production, medicine and labour. Most diseases can be prevented with a planned health programme drawn up with the farm's veterinarian.

Vaccination

Vaccines teach the animal's body to fight a disease before it meets it. Follow these rules:

  • Vaccinate according to the farm's written programme and the vet's advice.
  • Keep vaccines in the fridge (cold chain) and out of the sun. Never use expired or frozen vaccine.
  • Use the dose, route and booster interval on the label.
  • Use clean needles and change them often.
  • Record the date, product, batch number and animals treated.

Parasite control

  • Dip or pour-on for ticks according to the season and the tick load.
  • Deworm based on need, for example by using the FAMACHA eye-colour check in sheep and goats, rather than dosing the whole flock blindly. This slows down resistance.
  • Rotate camps so animals do not graze where parasite larvae are thick.

Biosecurity

  • Quarantine new animals in a separate camp for at least the period your vet recommends before mixing them.
  • Control visitors and vehicles; use foot baths and wash wheels where needed.
  • Fix fences to keep out stray and wild animals.
  • Remove and safely dispose of carcasses, afterbirth and dead animals.

Hygiene and management

  • Clean water troughs and feed bunks regularly.
  • Keep pens and kraals dry and clean.
  • Give balanced feed and the right licks for the season.
  • Do not overcrowd.

Daily observation is part of prevention. Count the animals, watch them walk, eat and drink. An animal that stands alone, does not eat or walks stiffly should be checked straight away.

lessons.title: Recognising sick animals and giving treatment
lessons.html:
Signs of a sick animal

Learn what normal looks like so that you can see when something is wrong.

HealthyPossibly sick
Alert, bright eyesDull, head down, stands alone
Eats and chews the cudNot eating, not ruminating
Normal dungDiarrhoea, blood in dung, no dung
Normal breathingFast breathing, coughing, nasal discharge
Moves freelyLame, stiff, swollen joints

Check temperature with a thermometer in the rectum. A raised temperature often means infection. Report your findings to the farm manager or vet.

Treating animals safely

  1. Get a diagnosis from the vet or a trained person. The wrong medicine wastes money and can do harm.
  2. Read the label. Use the correct dose for the animal's mass, the correct route (under the skin, into the muscle, by mouth or pour-on) and the correct injection site.
  3. Restrain the animal properly in a crush or with enough helpers.
  4. Complete the full course, especially with antibiotics.
  5. Isolate the sick animal in a sick pen with feed, water and shade.
  6. Record the treatment, date, product and withdrawal period.

Withdrawal periods

After many medicines, milk and meat may not be sold for a set time. Always follow the product label or your vet for the withdrawal period. Selling products from treated animals too early breaks the law and puts consumers at risk.

Safety

  • Wear gloves when handling dips, pour-ons and sick animals.
  • Never open the carcass of an animal that died suddenly - it may be anthrax, which can kill people. Report it.
  • Store medicines locked up and away from children and food.
  • Dispose of needles in a sharps container.

Key points

  • Bacteria, viruses, parasites, poor nutrition and poisons cause most disease.
  • Vaccination, parasite control and biosecurity prevent most losses.
  • Notifiable diseases must be reported to the state vet.
  • Treat only according to the label or vet, and keep records.
  • Respect withdrawal periods for milk and meat.
